causalMechanism.primaryVector: Orbitopathy and tear-film sequence: in service-connected hyperthyroidism due to Graves' disease, thyroid-stimulating-hormone-receptor autoantibodies activate orbital fibroblasts, driving glycosaminoglycan and hyaluronan deposition, adipogenesis, and cytokine-mediated orbital inflammation. The resulting proptosis, eyelid retraction, restrictive myopathy, and widened palpebral fissure increase the exposed ocular surface area and reduce the completeness of eyelid closure, so the tear film destabilizes and evaporates faster than the lacrimal system can replace it; lymphocytic infiltration and dysfunction of the lacrimal and accessory glands further reduce aqueous secretion, and the consequent ocular surface inflammation perpetuates tear-film instability and punctate epithelial damage. Selter et al. (PMID 25584018) reviewed the relationship between Graves' ophthalmopathy and dry eye syndrome and concluded that an increased risk of dry eye syndrome exists in patients with thyroid disease, describing a complex and bidirectional clinical relationship. Rana et al. (PMID 35167950) reviewed ocular surface disease in thyroid eye disease and reported that the prevalence of ocular surface disease among thyroid eye disease patients is estimated to range from about 65 to 95 percent, and that ocular surface inflammation and multifactorial changes to ocular surface homeostasis contribute substantially alongside the anatomical proptosis and corneal exposure mechanism. McAlinden (PMID 26605355) provides the epidemiologic linkage in his overview of thyroid eye disease, reporting that approximately 60 percent of patients with hyperthyroidism develop thyroid eye disease and that among thyroid eye disease patients roughly 85 percent are hyperthyroid, 10 percent hypothyroid, and 5 percent euthyroid — the last figure being the critical limitation for this theory. Framing under 38 CFR § 3.310: this is a § 3.310(a) direct-causation theory, in which the service-connected hyperthyroidism is asserted to have caused dry eye syndrome as an orbital and ocular-surface manifestation of the same autoimmune process. It is not a § 3.310(b) aggravation theory; aggravation would be the correct theory only where the record documents dry eye syndrome predating the thyroid disease and the claim is that the thyroid orbitopathy worsened a baseline tear-film disorder, in which case the attributable increment must be separated from the natural progression of that baseline condition and § 3.310(b) governs. Chronology and the individual analysis under § 3.310(a) or (b) require that the hyperthyroidism or Graves' disease diagnosis, and ideally thyroid-stimulating-hormone-receptor antibody status, precede or coincide with the onset of dry eye symptoms and objective ocular surface signs such as reduced tear break-up time, positive ocular surface staining, or Schirmer testing, so that the examiner can state that the dry eye syndrome is at least as likely as not caused by the service-connected hyperthyroidism — an opinion requiring a documented temporal sequence, an accounting for competing causes, and an approximate balance of evidence consistent with § 3.102. Competing causes that must be weighed include age-related tear deficiency, meibomian gland dysfunction and blepharitis, contact-lens wear, environmental exposure and screen-related tear evaporation, systemic medications such as antihistamines, tricyclic antidepressants, and isotretinoin, Sjögren's syndrome and other autoimmune sicca disease, diabetes mellitus, and prior ocular surgery or radiation. A further individualized caution: because thyroid eye disease and dry eye can occur in euthyroid and hypothyroid patients, the presence of dry eye in a veteran with treated thyroid disease does not by itself establish causation, and the nexus opinion must tie the ocular surface disease to the Graves' autoimmune process rather than to thyroid hormone levels alone. No individual probability is asserted here. Rating discipline under § 4.14: where dry eye has produced visual impairment that is separately rated under DCs 6061 through 6066 or under another § 4.79 code, the same impairment may not be rated a second time, and DC 7900 Note (2) and DC 7903 Note (3) both contemplate a single coordinate evaluation under § 4.79 for the eye involvement.

Primary condition: Service-connected hyperthyroidism, including Graves' disease, with documented thyroid-stimulating-hormone-receptor antibody positivity or clinical thyrotoxicosis
Primary diagnostic-code proposal: 38 CFR § 4.119, DC 7900 (hyperthyroidism, including, but not limited to, Graves' disease): 30 percent for six months after initial diagnosis, with residuals of disease or complications of medical treatment thereafter rated within the appropriate diagnostic code in the appropriate body system; Note (2) expressly directs that eye involvement occurring as a manifestation of Graves' disease be separately evaluated as diplopia (DC 6090), impairment of central visual acuity (DCs 6061 through 6066), or under the most appropriate diagnostic codes in § 4.79
Secondary condition: Dry eye syndrome (keratoconjunctivitis sicca and thyroid-eye-disease-associated ocular surface disease) in a veteran with service-connected hyperthyroidism
Secondary diagnostic-code proposal: 38 CFR § 4.79, DC 6025 (disorders of the lacrimal apparatus (epiphora, dacryocystitis, etc.)): 20 percent bilateral and 10 percent unilateral; where punctate corneal epithelial disease is documented, DC 6001 (keratopathy) is also available and is evaluated under the General Rating Formula for Diseases of the Eye, subject to the prohibition on pyramiding the same visual impairment under § 4.14. Qualified-human rating review required; a clinically justified analogous evaluation under §§ 4.20 and 4.27 may be required where the predominant disability picture is tear-film failure without a lacrimal-apparatus diagnosis
Original nexus theory: Causation

Legal boundary: § 3.310(a) concerns proximate causation; § 3.310(b) concerns attributable worsening beyond natural progression against a qualifying baseline. The at least as likely as not standard requires individual evidence and competing causes to be weighed. Apply claim-period rating criteria and § 4.14 nonpyramiding.
